references.text: Earlier in the same chapter, the instruction is given to choose a lamb for each household, which verse 5 elaborates with specific requirements.
At the consecration of priests, an unblemished animal (תָּמִים) is also required, showing that the requirement for flawlessness applies to all holy offerings.
The burnt offering must be a male without blemish (תָּמִים זָכָר) from the cattle, following the same principle of unblemishedness as the Passover lamb.
Sacrificial animals from the small livestock (כְּבָשִׂים or עִזִּים) must be a male without blemish, parallel to the requirements for the Passover lamb.
Detailed requirements state that sacrificial animals must be unblemished males from cattle, sheep, or goats to be accepted.
A one-year-old lamb without blemish (כֶּבֶשׂ תָּמִים בֶּן־שְׁנָתוֹ) is required as a burnt offering, the same age as the Passover lamb.
The daily burnt offering requires two one-year-old lambs without blemish, confirming the standard set in Exodus 12:5.
Ezekiel's future temple vision requires an unblemished young bull, continuing the principle of flawless sacrificial animals.
Christ is described as a spotless and unblemished lamb (ἀμνοῦ ἀμώμου καὶ ἀσπίλου), fulfilling the typology of the Passover lamb.
Christ offered himself without blemish (ἄμωμον) to God, as the perfect antitype to the unblemished Passover lamb.
John the Baptist points to Jesus as the Lamb of God (ὁ ἀμνὸς τοῦ θεοῦ) who takes away the sin of the world, a clear reference to Passover.
Confirms the theological principle that all sacrificial animals (sheep or goat) must be unblemished to be accepted by God.
